newsitem.title: UK: UK's FTSE 100 seen lower, Dow tumbles on rate woes.
newsitem.headline: UK's FTSE 100 seen lower, Dow tumbles on rate woes.

text.p: ** UK shares are expected to open around 25 pts lower on
Monday after Dow slides 139 pts or 1.89 pct amid nerves
over possible rate rise by Fed on Tuesday.
** UK gilts seen lower after U.S. bond market weakness.
** British Airways yr pre-exceptional profit 640 million stg.

UK shares were expected to open lower on Monday, taking their lead from a setback on Wall Street ahead of the weekend over worries that the Federal Reserve's open market committee will tighten monetary policy on Tuesday.

"Some of the bravado that the market was feeling on the possibility that Greenspan wouldn't put up rates is evaporating," said one equity salesman. "The market is now preparing itself for a quarter percent increase and anything different from that would really twitch us," he added.
"I expect a modest markdown, a dealer said. "But if we catch the market in the wrong mood it could be pushed quite hard."
"Market makers would dearly love to get this market down to start closing the shorts at lower levels," the dealer added.

On Friday the leading FTSE 100 index closed up 12.7 points at a record 4,693.9, its ninth record in 11 sessions. Stock shortages, especially in the financials, continued to lift prices and news of the planned Grand Metropolitan and Guinness merger helped revive takeover rumours.

But jitters over the U.S. policy meeting on Tuesday took their toll on U.S stocks. Triggered by a stronger than expected rise in U.S. housing starts and led by bond market weakness, the Dow eventually finished 139 points or 1.89 pct lower at 7,195.
The Dow was trading down 46 points as London closed.

UK gilt futures were expected to open lower, tracking weakness in U.S. bonds on Friday. Trade was expected to be thin ahead of the FOMC meeting and with much of Continental Europe on holiday, but UK PSBR data at 0830 GMT will help set direction. A deficit of 1.7 billion stg is expected.

Elsewhere, British Airways reported annual profits of 640 million stg, excluding exceptional items, topping most analysts expectations. The company made an exceptional charge of 127 million stg to cover restructuring costs associated with its "Business Efficiency" programme.
The company also wrote back in an exceptional gain of 125 million stg by restating its investment in USAirways.

Press reports that Britain's largest diversified industrial Lonrho, is in merger talks with South African mining house JCI, could also raise interest. Lonrho has a market capitalisation, based on Friday's closing share price of 135p of 1,062.3 million stg and the merger would create one of the world's largest mining groups.
But traders said the stock is no longer widely held. "A lot of the mainstream funds have avoided Lonrho over the last few years, it has always been seen as a risky one."

News that the new Labour government has called in water industry chiefs for an emergency conference on Monday to tackle the worst drought the country has faced in 200 years could prompt a reaction from the sector's shares, traders said.

"The government is going to be wagging its finger at the water companies at the emergency conference," said the equity salesman. "No-one loves the sector at the moment...it will be difficult for the (water chiefs) to say "we are doing are best" when they are losing 40 percent of the water through leaks in the pipes."
Among stocks trading ex-dividend today are Allied Domecq, BOC, Royal Bank of Scotland, Sainsbury, Whitbread and Tate and Lyle. Together they will take 3.55 points of the FTSE 100 index.
--Elaine Hardcastle, London Newsroom +44 171 542 4027
